content: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) refers to the reestablishment of sustained, effective cardiac activity that is capable of maintaining adequate perfusion, accompanied by significant respiratory effort, following a cardiac arrest. The likelihood of achieving ROSC is significantly improved through the administration of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation. A phenomenon known as the Lazarus phenomenon, or autoresuscitation, describes the spontaneous return of circulation after resuscitation efforts have been discontinued in a patient experiencing cardiac arrest. Hyperthermia, or elevated body temperature, is observed in approximately 42% of patients following cardiac arrest and is associated with worse neurological outcomes and a poor overall prognosis. As part of post-cardiac arrest care, induced therapeutic hypothermia is often employed to mitigate these adverse effects. The development of fever after cardiac arrest is believed to result from an early systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Cardiac arrest leads to ischemia and subsequent reperfusion injury throughout the body, which triggers a robust inflammatory response. Patients who survive cardiac arrest frequently exhibit elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, dysregulated cytokine production, and increased plasma endotoxins. These immunological abnormalities closely resemble those observed in sepsis.
